opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the breadth isn't really a flaw in the data. It's telling you something true about the state of knowledge. When you take everyone's individual forecasts and average them into one distribution, you get something very spread out, often with meaningful probability on a milestone arriving within a decade and also substantial probability on it taking many decades or longer. I read that as a fairly honest picture of deep uncertainty, both within individual researchers and across the field.

A few things are going on there. One is that individuals themselves often give wide distributions. People aren't usually saying "it'll happen in exactly 2040." They're saying it might be soon, it might be a long way off, and they're spreading their probability accordingly. That seems reasonable to me given how hard this is to predict.

The other is that there's a lot of disagreement between people. Some respondents expect things very soon and others expect them very late, and averaging those together produces a distribution wider than many of the individual ones. So the aggregate is partly a measure of how little consensus there is.

I'd also caution against reading too much precision into any single number, like the median year. We've seen that the answers are quite sensitive to framing. If you ask people "in what year will there be a 50% chance" versus "what's the probability by a given year," you get noticeably different answers. And if you ask about automating all occupations versus achieving "high-level machine intelligence," which in principle should be closely related, you can get answers decades apart. That tells you people haven't thought this through to a consistent, settled view, which isn't surprising. These are researchers whose expertise is building systems, not forecasting decades out.

So how should someone use this? I wouldn't treat it as an oracle. But I think it's quite informative in a particular way: it says the people closest to the technology don't rule out transformative AI arriving fairly soon. If a large fraction of experts put real probability on major milestones in the next couple of decades, that's decision-relevant even if you're unsure of the exact timing. The wide range is itself the message. We should be preparing for a world where this could come relatively quickly, while acknowledging we really don't know.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers disagree about timing and that averaging produces a distribution wider than many individual forecasts, but it does not describe individually narrow forecasts centered on different times.

r002.rationale: It says individual researchers often give wide distributions, allowing for milestones soon or many decades later, and treats that as uncertainty within their forecasts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the width of those ranges is itself one of the main findings. When you aggregate across hundreds of researchers and you get a distribution for something like high-level machine intelligence where there's a meaningful chunk of probability on it happening within ten or fifteen years, and also a meaningful chunk on it being more than a century out, that's telling you the field doesn't actually know. People sometimes read the median off and say "experts predict AI by such-and-such year," and I think that misses the point. The median is one number from a very flat, very spread-out distribution, and the spread is the more honest summary.

Part of why it's so wide is that you're combining uncertainty at two levels. Each individual gives us a fairly uncertain distribution, often putting ten percent on one date and ninety percent on a date many decades later. And then on top of that, people disagree a lot with each other. So when you average, you get something that's wide both because individuals are unsure and because the population is unsure in different directions.

I'd also say the ranges are probably, if anything, too narrow in some respects, because we know the answers are sensitive to things they shouldn't be sensitive to. Framing effects are large. If you ask "by what year is there a fifty percent chance" versus "what's the probability by 2040," you get systematically different answers, sometimes decades apart. Asking about high-level machine intelligence versus full automation of labor, which are arguably describing nearly the same thing, gives you very different timelines. So if people's answers move that much based on wording, I think you should treat the whole exercise as a measure of informed intuition rather than careful calculation, and widen your own uncertainty accordingly.

The thing I take away from it is less a specific prediction and more that the people building these systems consider very fast progress a live possibility, and very slow progress a live possibility, and they don't feel they can rule either out. That's a strange situation to be in for a technology this consequential, and I think it should make us less confident in anyone, including the researchers themselves, who speaks as though the timeline is settled.

r001.rationale: The response says the aggregate is wide because researchers are uncertain and disagree, but it does not explain that averaging individually narrow forecasts centered on different times can produce a broad distribution.

r002.rationale: The response says individual researchers often give uncertain forecasts, assigning probability to dates many decades apart.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things going on that are worth distinguishing. One is uncertainty on the part of individual researchers, and the other is disagreement between researchers. You can get a very broad distribution by averaging together people who are each quite confident but have very different views about when something will happen. So you shouldn’t read the aggregate as though it represents a typical researcher’s uncertainty.

But I think the overall takeaway is that there isn’t a very settled view of these timelines. The forecasts put weight on quite different possibilities, and focusing on a single date—say, the date where the average distribution reaches fifty percent—can obscure that. It’s a useful summary, but it isn’t a deadline, or a date that everyone agrees on.

r001.rationale: It says the aggregate can be broad because researchers are individually confident but differ about when the milestone will occur.

r002.rationale: It mentions uncertainty among individual researchers as one possible source, but does not say their forecasts for human-level machine intelligence or full labor automation are often broad.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing to keep in mind is that those ranges combine two different kinds of uncertainty. Individual researchers are uncertain about when a milestone will happen, but researchers also disagree with one another. When you average their probability distributions, you get something that reflects both of those things.

So a broad distribution doesn’t necessarily mean that a typical researcher thinks almost any date is equally plausible. You could have one person who’s fairly confident it will happen soon and another who’s fairly confident it will happen much later, and the average will look quite spread out. To understand what’s going on, you’d want to look at the individual distributions as well.

I’d take the broad ranges as a reason to be cautious about treating any particular year as the prediction. There’s a lot of uncertainty here, and the average isn’t necessarily a view that any one researcher holds.

r001.rationale: It explains that researchers may each be fairly confident in different timelines, while averaging their distributions produces a spread-out aggregate.

r002.rationale: It says researchers are individually uncertain in general, but does not specifically state that forecasts for human-level machine intelligence or full labor automation are often broad.
